Section B
Directions: In this section, you are going to read a passage with ten statements attached to it. Each statement contains information given in one of the paragraphs. Can playing video games help you get a better job?
阅读说明：本文为 2019 年报道背景，受访者的职业经历、公司设想和个人归因不代表普遍因果结论；2017 年试验测量自报技能，并未验证就业结果。MBA 为比喻，放疗句改为限制健康组织所受照射。
A) The gaming industry attracts a wide audience, yet few of us are likely to list our achievements in playing computer games as work experience in our resume. But why not? Some businesses are waking up to the skills gamers can bring to the workplace.
B) One start-up is convinced that the skills learned by playing games — hard-won through years of training and battle — can be applied to real-life work situations. In the original 2019 report, Game Academy argued that its analysis of gaming preferences and occupations supported this belief. Such associations do not show that playing a game causes professional competence. Do you enjoy unusual puzzle games like Portal, or tower defence games like Defense Grid? The team reported that IT workers play those more than average. But if you prefer Civilization, Total War, or X-Com, where strategy and resource management are key, then, according to its analysis, your preferences might resemble those of managers.
C) Game Academy's idea is simple: analyse gamers’ habits from their online gaming profile, and offer courses in valuable skills that reflect their aptitudes — skills they can practise and refine in-game. Whether particular skills transfer to a job still requires evidence.
D) The original report also described military interest in relevant gaming skills. “The ability to absorb information, react swiftly and coordinate actions whilst remaining calm under pressure are often attributes of people that are good at gaming,” according to a Royal Air Force spokesperson. Those skills are part of what the Royal Air Force is looking for “in a variety of roles”. “Skills acquired through gaming can be very relevant to certain areas.”
E) “There are plenty of soft skills that gamers can utilise in a professional setting, such as teamwork, problem solving and strategic planning,” says Ryan Gardner, a regional director with Hays recruitment. But does that really mean your top 100 ranking in Overwatch should go down in your resume? “It’s about how you either make it relevant to the job you are applying for, or how it makes you more interesting as a potential employee,” Mr. Gardner says.
F) In 2017, a University of Glasgow randomized study reported improvements in students’ self-rated communication, adaptability and resourcefulness after eight weeks of selected games. It did not measure subsequent job offers. But “the research hasn’t really changed minds, at least not yet,” says the author of the study, Dr. Matthew Barr. The 2019 report described him as writing a book on the topic. “For now, I think the negative reputation around games means that telling someone you’re a determined gamer is more likely to harm your chances of getting a job. But if someone can explain how they’ve led a team in an online game, for example, they may be able to persuade an employer that this is useful,” says Dr Barr.
G) Playing games casually is unlikely to help your career prospects. But part of Game Academy’s suggestion is to transform casual gamers into “conscious” ones, applying critical thinking to developing their skills. “We see gameplay as a resource of talent,” says co-founder David Barrie. “Why can’t we put in our resume our gaming victories and achievements?” he asks. “If they say they want leadership — why can’t I point to my years of leading World of Warcraft raids?”
H) There are already plenty of gamers out there who know that their hobby has made them who they are. Earlier in 2019, Matthew Ricci told gaming site Kotaku: “If you're playing EVE Online you basically already have an MBA.” This is his analogy, not an academic qualification. Often made fun of in gaming circles as a “spreadsheet simulator (电子表格模拟器)”, the economy of the fictional EVE universe is driven by real market principles. If you want to build a new spaceship, the raw material has to be mined by another player. Manufacturing costs come into effect, and commodities fluctuate in price based on demand and the distance to haul the commodity.
I) Mr. Ricci, who had always dreamed of being the boss of his own company, ran an in-game corporation comprising hundreds of players. Eventually, he realised he could transfer his skills to real-life business — instead of doing it for free. He restructured Zentech, once a taxation vehicle for his father’s business, and, at the time of the 2019 report, it was in its fourth year helping international brands enter the Canadian market. EVE teaches skills like creativity, leadership, organisation, and conflict resolution, he maintains. He credits his success to his family, his strong desire to run his own business - and “a damn good company in Iceland that made a damn good game”.
J) Digital entrepreneur and business consultant Mia Bennett says: “In more traditional settings, gaming is still imagined to be the pursuit of teenage boys — a waste of time.” But there are some links to skills like “decision-making, the ability to anticipate and future planning,” she says. “It also helps with meta-skills — learning how to learn, experimentation, and creative thinking.”
K) At the time of the 2019 report, twelve years into his career, Mark Long, a radiotherapy physicist with the NHS in Surrey, had less time for games than earlier in his career. “I would love to say that my gaming skills allow me to destroy cancer using linear accelerators like photon (光子) blasters, but that’s not quite the reality.” Instead, he credits old-school games like Palace of Magic with exposing him to computers. Every new gaming upgrade improved his knowledge of how they worked. Gaming also encouraged a competitive spirit — and that, he believes, translates. He explains that treatment planning aims to optimize the radiation dose to the tumour while limiting exposure of healthy surrounding tissues and organs. It’s about “repeating the process, but each time doing something slightly different to improve the result”. Not unlike achieving a high score or a perfect run. “Most videogames are essentially puzzles to solve,” he says. “And problem-solving is a big part of my job.”
L) Over at Game Academy, Mr. Barrie is aware they still have a mountain to climb. “The employer community will need the science,” he says, but confesses he only became a true believer when he started asking players about their biggest in-game achievements. “The scale and scope of their answers were amazing,” he says. “But ask them the same about their work, and they don’t know.” “The engagement and powerful skills that people get playing a game — why can’t work be like that?” he asks.

Passage One
Questions 46 to 50 are based on the following passage.
研究说明：2016 年研究涉及一所学校两届共 536 名八年级学生，主要行为终点为次日零食饮料选择；不能由此断言长期预防肥胖。肥胖受饮食、活动等多因素影响。第 50 题答案同步限定证据范围。
Junk food is now a staple of many Americans’ diets. Some advertising campaigns from snack food companies, often featuring sports stars, send the message that we can neutralize any negative effects of consuming their products simply by getting more physical exercise. However, obesity has multiple influences, including diet, activity, sleep and genetics. Exercise is beneficial, but does not make every dietary pattern healthy.
Interventions (干预) to help reduce junk food consumption are especially important for children and teenagers. Prevention and effective treatment both matter. Unfortunately, while health education has shown some success among young children, teens have been harder to reach.
A 2016 study involving 536 eighth graders at one Texas school over two school years tried an innovative approach to change teenagers’ attitudes towards healthy eating, and the results are promising. The researchers argued that previous interventions have probably been unsuccessful because of a major flaw: they focused on a future, healthier you and assumed that this would be enough motivation for teenagers. In contrast, the new intervention cleverly exploits teenagers’ instinct for rebelliousness and autonomy, and the value they place on social justice.
To do this, researchers had students read an article on the food industry. The article described manipulative marketing, misleading health claims and efforts to make products harder to resist. It also criticized how advertising campaigns specifically target very young and poor people, causing harm for these vulnerable groups.
Afterwards, the treatment group read purported peer-survey results and comments about resisting food-company practices, then wrote their own responses. These materials were part of the intervention.
After the intervention, participants associated healthy eating with autonomy and social justice. The teenagers also rated healthy eating as being more appealing. Importantly, there were also some promising effects of the new intervention on actual behavior. A day later the students were offered a choice of snacks and drinks in a seemingly unrelated context. Compared with the controls, the treatment group made fewer unhealthy snack and drink choices overall. Linking eating choices to adolescents’ values may help motivate healthier choices, but the study did not establish lasting changes in diet or body weight.

A) They convey the idea that their products are ok if consumers exercise more.
B) They send the message that bad diets are responsible for Americans’ obesity.
C) They usually feature sports stars to emphasize the benefits of their snack foods.
D) They claim that lack of exercise is to blame for the increasing obesity rates.

B) It has placed much more emphasis on cure than on prevention.

D) It has found teenagers harder to reach than younger children.

C) They were based on the assumption that motivation was the only key.
D) They were incapable of appealing to teens’ instinct for rebelliousness.
49. How does the intervention appeal to teenagers’ desire for autonomy?
A) It emphasizes people’s sense of social responsibility.
B) It cleverly exploits teenagers’ personal weaknesses.
C) It presents food choices as a way to resist outside control.
D) It promises immediate rather than future benefit.
50. What conclusion can be drawn from the new research?
A) One lesson permanently removed the influence of snack-food advertising.
B) An effective intervention has to be found to persuade teenagers to switch to a healthier lifestyle.
C) Linking healthy eating to teenagers’ values improved next-day choices, but lasting effects remain unproven.
D) An innovative way to beat obesity is to expose food companies’ manipulative and deceptive practices.
Passage Two
Questions 51 to 55 are based on the following passage.
研究说明：无法从 REM 睡眠直接判定婴儿梦境，也没有“两岁才开始做梦”的确定共识。儿童梦境报告受年龄与收集方法影响，原 25%统计的分母和方向均有问题；第 51、52、54、55 题已同步订正。
Adults often report dreams after REM (rapid eye movement) sleep, though dreams can also occur in non-REM sleep. Infants spend a large share of sleep in an active state that develops into adult REM sleep. This alone does not tell us whether or what they dream.
Research links early REM sleep with developing brain connections. Its developmental functions do not settle questions about an infant's subjective experience; a sleeping baby cannot tell us what happened in a dream.
Nor can we confidently conclude that infants never have nightmares. In children and adults who can describe them, nightmares can be associated with stress or frightening experiences, including trauma (创伤), but there are other possible influences too.
What do babies dream about? The honest answer is that researchers do not know. Movements or facial expressions during sleep cannot give us a reliable account of dream content.
There is also no established age at which all children begin dreaming. Psychologist David Foulkes studied children's dream reports to understand how they develop. In a longitudinal laboratory study, he woke children three times on each study night and asked what they remembered.
His laboratory findings suggested that dream reports tend to become more detailed and complex as children grow. These are findings about reported experiences, not proof that an unreported dream did not occur.
Reports from some of the youngest children were brief, static snapshots (快照), often involving animals or familiar activities. Other studies using different methods have obtained richer reports, so these descriptions should not be treated as universal rules.
Older children in Foulkes' studies more often described action and connected events. Dream recall also changed with age. The original passage's claim that only 25 percent of the children failed to recall a dream misstates the evidence: the studies measured the proportion of awakenings yielding reports, and younger children often reported no dream.
If a baby appears distressed during sleep or upset on waking, other causes may be involved. That behavior alone neither proves nor rules out a dream.
51. What do scientists think of REM?
A) It is a sign of dreaming in adults and infants alike.
B) It is essential to human beings’ language learning.
C) It determines the formation of connections in the brain.
D) It is linked to early brain development, but cannot establish what infants dream.
52. What can we infer about nightmares from the passage?
A) They occur often in people with an active imagination.
B) Emotional stress can be one factor associated with them.
C) They vary in different stages of brain development.
D) They appear in the sleep of both adults and infants.
53. What is the aim of psychologist David Foulkes’ study?
A) To reveal the secrets of children's dreams.
B) To see if children start dreaming at age two.
C) To solve the mystery of dreaming and brain growth.
D) To confirm the general consensus on when kids dream.
54. What age-related pattern did Foulkes find in children’s dream reports?
A) They feature strange animals.
B) They are unsurprising to adults.
C) They tend to become more detailed and complex with age.
D) They reflect kids’ waking life.
55. What can we assume about babies who appear upset upon waking?
A) They have been roused against their will.
B) They have been disturbed by a nightmare.
C) They have trouble recollecting the images of their dreams.
D) Other factors may be involved; the behavior alone cannot establish a dream.
